---
title: "7.6 Count, ordinal, and nominal models"
---

- The summary recommendations from [Mize (2019)](https://sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/) in the last section apply to **any nonlinear effects**
  - These include nonlinear effects in linear regression models
  - It also includes all other categorical outcome models, like count, ordinal, and nominal models
- Count models are treated straightforwardly just like binary models
  - But, more potential prediction quantities to calculate effects
    - E.g., Predicted rate (count) and/or Pr(*y* = #)
- Ordinal and nominal models present multiple options
  - Interactions for effect on each outcome category separately
    - Proceed identically to binary models, but for all *L* outcome categories
  - Overall interaction effect across all outcome categories
    - Use total marginal effects to summarize overall effect of a focal IV

## Count models

- **Data**: Health and Retirement Study\* (older adults)
- **Outcome**: Count of functional limitations

> *We need to understand difficulties people may have with various activities because of a health or physical problem. Please tell me whether you have any difficulty doing each of the everyday activities that I read to you. Exclude any difficulties that you expect to last less than three months.*
>
> - *Walking several blocks*
> - *Walking one block*
> - *Walking across a room*
> - *Climbing several flights of stairs without resting*
> - *Climbing one flight of stairs without resting*
> - *Sitting for about two hours*
> - *Getting up from a chair after sitting for long periods*
> - *Stooping, kneeling, or crouching*
> - *Pulling or pushing large objects like a living room chair*

\*I'm pooling the waves and clustering the SEs on participant ID to account for repeated observations. For more serious analyses, I recommend a longitudinal/panel model

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

```{.stata-run}
(bin=54, start=0, width=.16666667)
```

![](fig/cda-07_06_a-hist_funclim.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.6.a] Histogram of the count of functional limitations (0 to 9) among older adults in the HRS: about 34% report 0, about 16% report 1, 11% report 2, and the percentages keep falling to about 2% reporting 9."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.6.a] Histogram of the count of functional limitations (0 to 9) among older adults in the HRS: about 34% report 0, about 16% report 1, 11% report 2, and the percentages keep falling to about 2% reporting 9."
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(sjmisc)          # frequency tables
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

hrs <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si.dta")

# Data management
hrs <- hrs[c("funclim", "age", "race4cat", "wealth_w", "collegeB", "marstatB", "woman",
  "hhidpn")]
hrs <- hrs[complete.cases(hrs), ]

# 7.6.a - distribution of outcome functional limiations count
ggplot(hrs, aes(x = funclim)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(100 * count / sum(count))), width = .3, fill = "gray60") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:9) +
  labs(title = "[7.6.a] Distribution of count of functional limitations (HRS; older adults)",
    x = "Functional limitations, count 0-9", y = "Percent")
```

:::

### HRS functional limitations example

- **Focal IV**: Age
  - Mean = 67
- **Moderating IV**: College degree (=1) or not (=0)
- **Controls**: Gender, marital status, race-ethnicity

> *RQ: How does aging affect physical health? Does aging have a different effect for those with and without college degrees?*
>
> *RQ: Will the physical health gap between those with and without college degrees be the same across different ages? How will it change at different ages?*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

```{.stata-run}
(bin=91, start=18, width=1)

```

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.6.b] Histogram of age (in one-year bins) among older adults in the HRS: few respondents are under 50; the frequency jumps to about 9,000 per year of age in the mid-50s to about 60, then declines steadily through the 70s and 80s, with few respondents past 95."
```

### Interaction effects on the rate

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. // Negative binomial count model for functional limitations.
. qui nbreg funclim c.age##i.collegeB i.race4cat i.marstatB i.woman, cluster(hhi
> dpn)

. est store flmod

```

## R

```{r}
# Treat binary/nominal variables as factors
hrs <- hrs |>
  mutate(across(c(collegeB, race4cat, marstatB, woman), as_factor))

# Negative binomial count model for functional limitations
flmod <- MASS::glm.nb(funclim ~ age * collegeB + race4cat + marstatB + woman, data = hrs)
```

:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
Ignore the coefficient on the interaction (product) term. Count models are nonlinear and coefficients are in a different metric than the predictions. Graph predictions and test interaction in MEs.
:::

- Graph the predictions for the count/rate

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. *7.6.c - Graph predicted rate/count of functional limitations
. est restore flmod
(results flmod are active now)

. qui margins collegeB, at(age=(45(2)95))

. marginsplot, ///
>     recastci(rline) ciopt(lpat(dash) col(*.5)) plotop(msym(none) lwid(*1.5)) /
> //
>     title("[7.6.c] Predicted number of functional limitations by age and colle
> ge", size(*1.1)) ///
>     ylab(0(1)5) ytitle("# of functional limitations") ///
>     xtitle("Age") legend(order(3 "No degree" 4 "College"))

Variables that uniquely identify margins: age collegeB

```

![](fig/cda-07_06_c-pr_funclim.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.6.c] Predicted number of functional limitations by age (45 to 95) for those with and without a college degree, with confidence intervals. Both rise with age at an increasing rate: without a degree from about 1.8 at 45 to about 4.2 at 95; with a degree from about 0.75 at 45 to about 4.3 at 95. The college advantage is large at younger ages and disappears by the mid-90s."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.6.c] Predicted number of functional limitations by age (45 to 95) for those with and without a college degree, with confidence intervals. Both rise with age at an increasing rate: without a degree from about 1.8 at 45 to about 4.2 at 95; with a degree from about 0.75 at 45 to about 4.3 at 95. The college advantage is large at younger ages and disappears by the mid-90s."
# 7.6.c - Graph predicted rate/count of functional limitations
# (one age at a time, which needs much less memory with 270,000+ observations)
pr <- bind_rows(lapply(seq(45, 95, 2), function(a) {
  avg_predictions(flmod, by = c("age", "collegeB"), vcov = ~hhidpn,
    newdata = datagrid(age = a, collegeB = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
}))

ggplot(pr, aes(x = age, y = estimate, color = collegeB, fill = collegeB)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = .2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = c("No degree", "College")) +
  scale_fill_discrete(labels = c("No degree", "College")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:5, limits = c(0, 5)) +
  labs(title = "[7.6.c] Predicted number of functional limitations by age and college",
    x = "Age", y = "# of functional limitations", color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. *AME of age for those w and w/o college degrees
. mecompare age, by(collegeB) amount(10) model(flmod)

Predicting: Predicted number of events
Marginal effects (N_flmod=273547)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
age + 10 (centered)              |                                       
                   no bachelor's |     1      0.461      0.010      0.000
            bachelor's or higher |     2      0.614      0.018      0.000

```

## R

```{r}
# Changes in continuous IVs centered on the observed values, like mecompare
options(marginaleffects_contrast_direction = "center")

# AME of age for those w and w/o college degrees
mes <- avg_comparisons(flmod, variables = list(age = 10), by = "collegeB",
  vcov = ~hhidpn, newdata = datagrid(collegeB = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
mes
```

:::

> *Aging 10 years predicts a 0.46 increase in the number of functional limitations for someone without a college degree. For someone with a college degree, the same 10-year increase in age predicts a 0.61 increase.*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. metest 2 - 1

                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
 age_collegeB_1 - age_collegeB_0 |     0.153      0.020      0.000 

```

## R

```{r}
hypotheses(mes, hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0")
```

:::

> *On average, aging has a significantly larger effect on the number of functional limitations for someone with a college degree than for someone without (p \< .001).*

- Given the substantial nonlinearities we see in the graph, good to report interaction at different ages and not only the average effect (above)
  - I've picked 3 theoretical ideal types of ages 45, 65, 85

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
With **mecompare**, use the **start()** option to specify conditional values of a focal IV

With **avg_comparisons**, in the **newdata = datagrid()**
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. *2nd diffs for age * college, at three ideal types of age
. mecompare age, by(collegeB) amount(10) start(age=(45 65 85)) model(flmod)

Predicting: Predicted number of events
Marginal effects (N_flmod=273547)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate  Robust SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
age + 10 (centered)              |                                       
             no bachelor's at 45 |     1      0.307      0.004      0.000
             no bachelor's at 65 |     2      0.437      0.009      0.000
             no bachelor's at 85 |     3      0.622      0.017      0.000
      bachelor's or higher at 45 |     4      0.257      0.003      0.000
      bachelor's or higher at 65 |     5      0.527      0.013      0.000
      bachelor's or higher at 85 |     6      1.080      0.045      0.000

```

```{.stata-run}
. qui metest, clear

. qui metest 1 - 4, add rowname("at age 45")

. qui metest 2 - 5, add rowname("at age 65")

. qui metest 3 - 6, add rowname("at age 85")

. metest, title("2nd diff. of effect of age for those w and w/o college degrees"
> )

2nd diff. of effect of age for those w and w/o college degrees

                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
                       at age 45 |     0.050      0.005      0.000 
                       at age 65 |    -0.090      0.015      0.000 
                       at age 85 |    -0.459      0.047      0.000 

```

## R

```{r}
# 2nd diffs for age * college, at three ideal types of age
mes <- avg_comparisons(flmod, variables = list(age = 10), by = c("collegeB", "age"),
  vcov = ~hhidpn, newdata = datagrid(collegeB = unique, age = c(45, 65, 85),
    grid_type = "counterfactual"))
mes

hypotheses(mes, hypothesis = ~ revpairwise | age)
```

:::

> *Those without college degrees acquire more functional limitations much earlier in life than those with college degrees. But by older ages, the groups converge.*
>
> *For individuals in their 40s, aging is associated with a faster increase in functional limitations for someone without a college degree. However, for someone in their 60s, those with college degrees experience a larger increase in functional limitations. By their 80s, the rate is much stronger for someone with a college degree.*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## Ordinal and nominal models

- With multi-outcome models, you can:
  - Test for interaction across each outcome category separately

> *RQ: Does parenthood have a different effect on "excellent" health for the married and the unmarried? On "good" health, etc.*

  - Or, aggregate up to total effects across each outcome category, for the effect on the DV as a holistic construct

> *RQ: Does parenthood have a different effect on health for the married and the unmarried?*

  - Or both

### GSS self-rated health example

- **Data**: GSS 2000 - 2021
- **DV**: Self-rated health

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear
(cda_gss.dta |  GSS 1972-2021 CDA - Categorical Data Analysis | date created 202
> 3)

. 
. **only keep var of interest
. drop if missing(healthR, married, parent, woman, race4, age)
(17,923 observations deleted)

. drop if year < 2000 | year > 2021
(29,261 observations deleted)

. 
. fre healthR

healthR -- Self-rated health
-----------------------------------------------------------------
                    |      Freq.    Percent      Valid       Cum.
--------------------+--------------------------------------------
Valid   1 Poor      |       1167       5.39       5.39       5.39
        2 Fair      |       4310      19.90      19.90      25.28
        3 Good      |      10569      48.79      48.79      74.07
        4 Excellent |       5616      25.93      25.93     100.00
        Total       |      21662     100.00     100.00           
-----------------------------------------------------------------

```

## R

```{r}
gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")

# only keep var of interest
gss <- gss[c("healthR", "married", "parent", "woman", "race4", "age", "year")]
gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss), ] |>
  filter(year >= 2000, year <= 2021)

frq(gss, healthR)
```

:::

- **Focal IV**: Parent (=1) or not (=0)
- **Moderating IV**: Married (=1) or not (=0)
- **Controls**: Age, gender, race-ethnicity
- **Model**: Using a multinomial logit model, as an ordinal model fails the Brant test, with meaningful differences in conclusions
  - Procedure for testing interactions is identical in nominal and ordinal models

### Interaction across each outcome category

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. *Fit nominal model w/ interaction
. qui mlogit healthR i.married##i.parent i.woman i.race4 c.age

. est store hmod

```

## R

```{r}
# Treat binary/nominal variables as factors
gss <- gss |>
  mutate(across(c(healthR, married, parent, woman, race4), as_factor)) |>
  droplevels()

# Fit nominal model w/ interaction
hlthmod <- nnet::multinom(healthR ~ married * parent + woman + race4 + age, data = gss,
  trace = FALSE)
```

:::

- Plot predictions **for each outcome category**, and **at each combination** of married and parent
  - Here, 4 \* (2\*2) = 16

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

![](fig/cda-07_06_e-pr_health.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.6.e] Dot plot of the predicted probability of each self-rated health category (poor, fair, good, excellent) for unmarried and married respondents, with and without children. Poor health is about .03 to .08, fair about .14 to .24, good about .47 to .50, and excellent about .20 to .33. Unmarried parents have higher probabilities of poor and fair health and a lower probability of excellent health than unmarried non-parents; among the married the parent and non-parent dots are closer together."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.6.e] Dot plot of the predicted probability of each self-rated health category (poor, fair, good, excellent) for unmarried and married respondents, with and without children. Poor health is about .03 to .08, fair about .14 to .24, good about .47 to .50, and excellent about .20 to .33. Unmarried parents have higher probabilities of poor and fair health and a lower probability of excellent health than unmarried non-parents; among the married the parent and non-parent dots are closer together."
# 7.6.e - Plot predictions at combos of married and parent, for each outcome
pr <- avg_predictions(hlthmod, by = c("married", "parent", "group"),
  newdata = datagrid(married = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) |>
  mutate(row = factor(paste0("Pr(", group, ")\n", married),
    levels = paste0("Pr(", rep(levels(gss$healthR), each = 2), ")\n",
      levels(gss$married))))

ggplot(pr, aes(x = estimate, y = row, color = parent)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    position = position_dodge(.4)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .6, .1), limits = c(0, .6)) +
  labs(title = "[7.6.e] Probability of self-rated health category, by marital and parental status",
    x = "Pr(Self-Rated Health)", y = NULL, color = NULL)
```

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.6.h] Two panels with a line at zero. Left: marginal effects of parental status on each self-rated health category for the unmarried and the married; for the unmarried, parenthood raises the probabilities of poor, fair, and good health by about .02 each and lowers the probability of excellent health by about .06; for the married all four effects are near zero. Right: the second differences (married minus unmarried) are about -.022 for poor, -.004 for fair, -.019 for good, and .045 for excellent; the confidence intervals for poor and excellent exclude zero."
# 7.6.f - MEs of parental status
mes <- avg_comparisons(hlthmod, variables = "parent", by = c("group", "married"),
  newdata = datagrid(married = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"))

# 2nd diffs for married X parent
sec_ds <- hypotheses(mes, hypothesis = ~ pairwise | group)

# 7.6.h - Combine MEs and 2nd diff plot
panels <- c("Marginal effects of parental status", "2nd Differences (Married * Parent)")
both <- bind_rows(
  mes |> mutate(panel = panels[1], row = paste0("Pr(", group, ")\n", married)),
  sec_ds |> mutate(panel = panels[2], row = paste0("Pr(", group, ")"))) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panels),
    row = factor(row, levels = rev(c(paste0("Pr(", rep(levels(gss$healthR), each = 2), ")\n",
      levels(gss$married)), paste0("Pr(", levels(gss$healthR), ")")))))

ggplot(both, aes(x = estimate, y = row)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-.1, .1, .05), limits = c(-.1, .1)) +
  labs(title = "[7.6.h] Marginal effects of parental status (left), and 2nd differences",
    subtitle = "2nd difference is difference in size of parent gap, across marital statuses",
    x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

:::

> *"The interaction effect can be tested as the second difference or equality of the two MEs of parental status---for the unmarried and the married---for each outcome (Mize 2019). The right panel of Figure 8 shows the second difference for each outcome category. Two of the four are significant, indicating that parental status has a larger effect for unmarried than for married individuals on the probability of reporting poor or excellent health (though in opposite directions). We find no evidence of interaction for the probability of reporting fair or good health."* ([Mize and Han 2025](/research/mize_han_socsci_2025.qmd), p.146)

### Total marginal effects

- Although the approach above provides a valid test of interaction, it provides an ambiguous answer given differences across outcome categories
  - In addition, it answers a more nuanced question than *"is the effect of parental status on health the same for married and unmarried individuals?"*
- If this broader question is of interest, total MEs can provide a holistic quantification of the effect of parental status to use in the test of interaction
  - In this case, we calculate two total MEs of parental status, one for the married and one for the unmarried, and then test their equality using a second difference test
- With multi-outcome models, an IV's total effect is its holistic effect across all outcomes
  - The **total ME** statistic is the sum of all the marginal effects for that IV (using absolute values) divided by two

$$total\ ME = \frac{\sum_{\lambda = 1}^{\Lambda}\left|\eta_{\lambda}(x_{k} = end, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k}^{*}) - \eta_{\lambda}(x_{k} = start, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k}^{*})\right|}{2}$$

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
# Total ME functions
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tdmize/Rfunctions/main/ME_helper_functions.R")

# Calculate Total MEs to simplify interaction test
tme <- avg_comparisons(hlthmod, variables = "parent", by = "married",
  newdata = datagrid(married = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  hypothesis = totalme(hlthmod))
tme
```

:::

> *The total effect of parental status is 0.061 for the unmarried; that is, parents and non-parents differ by about 6 percentage points total in terms of their self-rated health. For the married, the total effect of parenthood is only 0.017.*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
hypotheses(tme, hypothesis = ~ pairwise)
```

:::

> *Parental status has a larger total effect for the unmarried than for the married; that is, in terms of self-rated health, parental status matters more for those who are unmarried than for those who are married (2^nd^ diff. = -0.044, p \< .01).*
